findings.description: The new Bash hidden-name matcher misses discovery commands such as `grep -rn hidden .` and `find . -iname '*hidden*'`. It also misses mixed-case path references such as `cat /workspace/Hidden/tests.json`, despite the documented case-insensitive check.
findings.failure_mode: An agent can search for or read hidden evaluation material without the grader recording a hidden contamination hit, allowing contaminated results into the evaluation.
findings.suggested_fix: Recognize hidden-related command arguments and case variants while excluding prose through shell context rather than punctuation alone.

findings.description: All heredoc bodies are discarded from path scanning, but unquoted heredocs execute command substitutions. For example, `cat <<EOF\n$(cat /root/secret.txt)\nEOF` actually reads the outside file, yet its only outside path is removed before scanning.
findings.failure_mode: Outside-sandbox reads executed within an unquoted heredoc are graded as uncontaminated.
findings.suggested_fix: Distinguish quoted from unquoted heredoc delimiters and retain executable substitutions in unquoted bodies for contamination scanning.

findings.description: The blanket `"=" in w` exemption assumes that paths cannot contain equals signs. Equals signs are valid in Linux filenames, so `cat /home/operator/notes=secret.txt` is skipped even though it is an absolute path outside the allowed roots.
findings.failure_mode: Reading an outside file whose pathname contains `=` produces no outside_path contamination hit.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the blanket exemption and identify assignment or regex syntax from the surrounding shell token; preserve absolute path candidates containing `=`.

findings.description: Counting single and double quotes independently misinterprets quotes inside another quoted string. In `echo "it's"; ls /root`, the apostrophe makes `in_quotes` return true for the unquoted `/root` argument, causing check_value to discard that sensitive path.
findings.failure_mode: Ordinary preceding command text can suppress detection of a subsequent outside-path access.
findings.suggested_fix: Track shell quoting and escaping state, treating an apostrophe inside double quotes as literal text, and apply the exemption only when the candidate is actually quoted.

findings.description: HEREDOC is compiled with re.S, so `.` inside `(?:.*?\n)*?` also matches newlines. The inner `.*?\n` and the outer `*?` are ambiguous over the same newlines (and `\s*` before `\2` can eat newlines too). When no terminator line matches, Python's backtracking regex tries every composition of the remaining lines: 2^(lines-1) attempts. Triggers seen in real transcripts: an unterminated heredoc (model truncation, `EOF;` or `EOF)` on the terminator line), a here-string `cat <<< word` followed by more lines (`<<` + space + `word` is accepted as a heredoc header), or a conflict marker `<<<<<<< HEAD` inside a script the agent writes. A 30-line tail is ~1e9 steps; 40 lines never finishes.
findings.failure_mode: strip_heredocs() hangs on one Bash tool_use value; contamination() never returns, the grade for the run (and the batch driver waiting on ablation-grade.sh) stalls until the watchdog/timeout, and the run is rowed infrastructure_error or interrupted with no diagnostic.

findings.description: HEREDOC matches `[^\n]*\n` after the delimiter, i.e. the rest of the header line, and the whole match is replaced by `<<HEREDOC`. The path-word scan (ABS_WORD and HOME_WORD on `body`) therefore never sees anything written after the heredoc operator on that line. `cat <<EOF > /root/.ssh/authorized_keys`, `cat <<'EOF' > /home/other/x`, `cat <<EOF >> ~/.bashrc` (host mode) all lose their redirect target. The header says only heredoc bodies are stripped; the redirect target is a path the agent reached, not data.
findings.failure_mode: A write outside the sandbox via the common `cmd <<EOF > /abs/path` idiom is not reported as outside_path; the run grades as not contaminated.

findings.description: Confirms reviewer concern 1. In Bash text `hidden` only counts as HIDDEN or when glued to `/ . _ = -`. The most natural discovery probes are plain words: `grep -rn hidden .`, `grep -ri hidden`, `find . -name '*hidden*'` (adjacent chars are `*`), `ls -la | grep -i hidden`, `rg hidden`. None match. The motivating false positive was prose inside a heredoc, but heredoc stripping (strip_heredocs) already exists and is not used for this check; the token rule overshoots and exempts exactly the commands the scan exists to catch.
findings.failure_mode: An agent that greps or finds for hidden tests is not flagged `hidden`; contaminated runs are counted as clean and inflate recall/hidden_tests.
findings.suggested_fix: For Bash, run the plain `"hidden" in strip_heredocs(val).lower()` check on the command text (heredoc bodies removed), and apply HIDDEN_TOKEN only to the stripped heredoc bodies if a prose exemption is still wanted. Add tests for `grep -rn hidden .` and `find . -name '*hidden*'` → hidden.

findings.description: Confirms reviewer concern 2. in_quotes counts raw `'` and `"` independently with no awareness of nesting or escapes. An apostrophe inside a double-quoted string (`echo "Let's check"; ls /root`), `\"`, or `$'...'` flips parity for the rest of the command, and every following one-component sensitive word (/root, /home, /mnt, /media, /srv) is skipped at line 1444.
findings.failure_mode: `ls /root`, `ls /home` after any apostrophe in preceding text is not reported.
findings.suggested_fix: Use shlex-style scanning: walk body once tracking state (outside / in single / in double, honouring backslash in double quotes) and record quoted spans; test membership of m.start(1) in a span. Or drop the quote heuristic for sensitive single words and accept the `grep ' /tmp | /home '` false positive, which the comment already treats as marginal.

findings.description: Confirms reviewer concern 3. Any one-component absolute word outside SENSITIVE_SINGLE is treated as a slash command or regex delimiter: `ls /boot`, `ls /run`, `ls /snap`, `ls /data`, `ls /secrets`, `ls /Users` (macOS host mode) are all skipped before outside()/SENSITIVE ever see them. The whitelist of five names is a guess at data-holding roots; host-mode sandboxes in particular can have arbitrary top-level directories.
findings.failure_mode: Listing a top-level directory outside the allowed roots is not flagged.
findings.suggested_fix: Invert the rule: skip a one-component word only when it looks like a Loa slash command (`^/[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$` AND it is not preceded by a command word such as ls/cd/cat/find/stat/du/tree, or it appears in a known command list from .claude/commands), or when it is a `/x/` delimiter after s y = ~ '. Otherwise keep it a candidate and let outside() decide.

findings.description: Confirms reviewer concern 4. `"=" in w` discards a multi-component path if any component contains `=`, e.g. `cat /home/operator/notes=secret.txt` or `/root/env=prod/.env`. The comment's premise ("no path component carries =") is false; `=` is legal in file names and common in generated names.
findings.failure_mode: A path outside the sandbox that contains `=` is not reported.
findings.suggested_fix: Only treat `=` as a regex/key=value marker when it is in the first component (`^/[^/]*=`), which is where sed `s=/x=/y=` and `KEY=/value` shapes put it; keep later components as path.

findings.description: after_closing_quote treats any quote preceded by a non-delimiter character as a closing quote glued to a token. The delimiter set `=(<>|;&,` omits `[`, `{`, `:` and letters used as string prefixes, so an opening quote after those is misread: `python3 -c "for p in ['/root/.ssh/id_rsa']: ..."` (`[` before `'`), `f"/root/{u}/.bashrc"`, `r"/home/x"`, `{"/root/x"}`, `-C"/root"`. The word is then skipped at line 1442 even though it is a full absolute path.
findings.failure_mode: Absolute paths outside the sandbox inside Python list literals or f-strings/raw strings in a Bash `python -c` command are not reported.
findings.suggested_fix: Require the quoted segment to be a real path head: look back from pos-1 over the shell word and accept only if it ends in `$NAME"`, `${...}"`, `)"`, or a quoted segment that itself contains `/` (e.g. `re.search(r"(\$\w+|\}|\)|/[^\s'\"]*)['\"]$", body[:pos])`). Add `[`, `{`, `:` to the delimiter set at minimum.
